attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his April 14, 2026 newsletter post.

semantics.note: Keeps 'appears to have immediately', the tiers and the Plus scope. The 'appears' softens the link to the launch more than the existence of a reduction, so this is a scorable past observation.

contract.note: Reading this as Codex usage on Plus fits the context, which refers to bonus rate limits and '10x or 20x higher than plus'. Treating the end of the promotion and the rebalancing as a reduction in available usage is an ordinary reading. Not requiring proof that the launch caused it respects 'appears'.

evidence.note: OpenAI's dated April 9 release note announces the $100 tier. The same entry ends the Plus Codex promotion and moves Plus usage away from long single-day sessions. A company stating its own policy is the primary record here.

reviews.rationale: On the same day it launched the $100 Pro tier, OpenAI ended the temporary Plus Codex promotion and limited long, high-intensity Plus sessions. That reduced the usage available to $20 subscribers alongside the launch, which meets the support condition. The size of the cut and whether the launch independently caused it are not established, but the claim's hedged wording does not require either.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words, restating a view he says he has held for years.

semantics.note: A present causal claim: unreliable outputs and high costs make AI companies inherently unsustainable. The normalisation matches the statement.

contract.note: The plain reading (that these factors structurally prevent viable operation) is the ordinary meaning of 'inherently unsustainable'. The contract notes that no accounting basis is given, and it does not stretch the claim either way.

evidence.note: Documents real hallucination problems and adoption concerns, but has no economic test of sustainability.
Falling customer-facing inference prices qualify the cost argument, but they are not provider costs or proof of viability.
The Anthropic S-1, dated before the cutoff, shows improving margins alongside continuing losses and financing risk. It neither shows durable sustainability nor shows it is impossible.
OpenAI's CFO describes compute scarcity and revenue growth. This is a company self-description and does not settle unit economics.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows real reliability problems, falling prices, better margins and continuing losses. None of it shows that reliability and cost structurally prevent viability, and none shows a sustainable LLM business. The causal claim of inherent unsustainability is not settled by the evidence available by the cutoff.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in the April 14, 2026 post.

semantics.note: A compound observation: a firm benchmark-validity criticism, a firm 'nobody can explain' claim, and a hedged 'does not appear to extend' beyond coding. The hedged part is not scored; the firm parts are.

contract.note: Starting 'the last few months' in December 2025 is the evaluator's choice but reasonable for a post dated April 14. Reading 'nobody can explain' as the absence of any concrete demonstrated account is a fair reading of hyperbole. The contract splits the claim into components.

evidence.note: METR, independently, found automated SWE-bench passes about 24 points above maintainer merge rates. This supports the benchmark-versus-practice criticism, though it tested older models.

OpenAI's December 2025 disclosure gives a concrete, expert-judged account of non-coding gains such as spreadsheets and presentations. Vendor-run, but it is a documented explanation of what the improvement enables.
Outside experts confirmed a proof flaw that a model found. This is a concrete non-coding research result, but it has no comparison with earlier models, so it is context only.

reviews.rationale: The benchmark-validity part holds: METR shows automated passes overstate maintainer acceptance. The firm claim that nobody can explain what improvement yields fails, because a documented account of expert-judged non-coding gains existed in the window. That account comes from the vendor, but it still shows an explanation existed. The hedged 'does not appear to extend beyond coding' is not scored.

attribution.note: Zitron's own first-person account of his experience.

semantics.note: An autobiographical observation that keeps 'every time', the most powerful LLMs, and the highest-priced research tools.

contract.note: Limits the claim to his own sessions and requires authenticated session records. That is fair, though what counts as 'unique' remains for the reader to decide.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no evidence items. No records of Zitron's sessions, the tools used or their outputs were found, and other users' results cannot confirm or contradict his own experience. The evidence does not settle the claim.
